title: 21 Grams
full_review:
In a film about intersecting lives it seems only fitting that the pivotal tragedy fueling "21 Grams" (Focus) takes place at a crosswalk intersection.

As in his freshman effort, "Amores Perros" (2001), director Alejandro Gonzalez Inarritu interweaves disparate narrative strands into a tapestry of raw emotion, crafting a gritty and grim morality tale of three shattered souls linked by cataclysm which ruminates on the interconnectivity of people's lives. Buttressed by riveting performances from its ensemble cast, the film plumbs the depths of the human condition, exploring with unflinching emotional honesty themes of fate and faith, life and death, despair and hope, sin and redemption.

Like the anguished terrain of "Mystic River," "21 Grams" charts a course through a bleak landscape which is at times hard to watch. But one emerges from the taxing experience the better for it, haunted by its elegiac images long after leaving the theater.

Headlining the tragic triptych is Sean Penn as Paul Rivers, a timid, terminally-ill math professor awaiting a heart transplant. Though long depleted of affection, his strained marriage is prolonged by his wife's (Charlotte Gainsbourg) desire to get pregnant before he dies. Her ability to conceive, however, has been compromised by uterine damage procured during an earlier abortion, forcing the couple to resort to artificial insemination.

Paul gets a reprieve from his deathbed by way of a heart transplant. But his second lease on life comes at a great price, paid in tears by Cristina Peck (Naomi Watts), a recovering drug addict who loses her husband -- whose heart Paul receives -- and two young daughters in a tragic off-screen hit-and-run accident.
The driver of the car, Jack Jordan (Benicio Del Toro), is a volatile ex-con-turned-born-again-Christian struggling to hold down a steady job and provide for his family.

As Paul's marriage dissolves, he searches out information about his heart donor. His inquiry leads him to Cristina, who, inconsolably numb, is slipping back into the abyss of addiction. They become lovers and plot revenge against Jack, whose guilt preys on his conscience. Their trajectories converge in a nexus of rage and remorse.

Some viewers may, justifiably, find the palpably dark, almost funereal tone of "21 Grams" off-putting. However, it needs to be pointed out that the characters' self-destructive behavior -- including vengeful acts of violence, drug abuse and vacuous sex -- while not to be condoned, must be judged in the context of the characters' woundedness and thus viewed as desperate cries for psychological, emotional and most of all spiritual healing.

Peppered throughout the narrative are moments when the cloud cover of harsh reality is parted, allowing the film's overlying humanity to shine forth. Some indelible images include Cristina, grief-stricken and prostrate on the kitchen floor, replaying her husband's final message on her cell phone and Jack's tortured expression frozen by the knowledge that God's impenetrable gaze sees everything and even "knows the numbers of hairs on my head."

As in his film "Amores Perros," Inarritu constructs "21 Grams" in a fractured narrative style, jumping freely back and forth in time. The result is less a jigsaw puzzle than a mosaic, which when viewed in its entirety reveals a splendor greater than the sum of its parts. Though some may find its dizzying chronological leapfrogging confusing, the device never feels gimmicky.

At its core, this gripping film examines the ripple effects death has on the living, and imparts a message about forgiveness -- of others, and more importantly, of ourselves.

By the way, "21 Grams" refers to the weight a body loses at the moment of death; some attribute this to the weight of one's departing soul. A closing voiceover compares the postmortem variable to the weight of five nickels or a hummingbird -- a mass disproportionate to the weightiness of the film's subject matter. Just in case you were wondering, an Oscar weighs about eight pounds.

Due to several sexual encounters with partial nudity, recurring rough and crude language as well as profanity, some violence and drug abuse, a suicide attempt and a fleeting erotic image, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
